## What you will learn

- How cultivar coefficients are estimated from field data, and why the answer is a distribution, not one
  number: the GLUE method of DSSAT, here as a Python port (`glue.py`), for soybean and for a new maize hybrid.
- How to calibrate by hand against growth measured during the season, with the statistics the course uses.
- What a soil profile in DSSAT holds, how much water a soil can store for a crop, and how to build a profile
  from a soil survey sheet.
- How the water balance limits production: soil water layer by layer, the effect of the soil's storage,
  and automatic irrigation.

## 1. Estimating cultivar coefficients with GLUE

A cultivar's coefficients cannot be measured directly; they are estimated by running the model with many
candidate values and keeping those that reproduce field observations. DSSAT's tool for this is GLUE
(Generalized Likelihood Uncertainty Estimation), written in R ([DSSAT/glue](https://github.com/DSSAT/glue)).
The notebook uses a Python port of its method, `docs/notebooks/glue.py`, which follows the R files step by
step (the module docstring lists them).

### Estimating coefficients: the ideas

A model coefficient is estimated by changing it until the simulation matches measurements, which is only as good
as the measurements, the order and the error model. Three ideas from the course carry through this module:

- **Least squares and likelihood.** Fitting by hand usually minimizes an error measure such as the RMSE; GLUE
  instead asks how likely the measurements are under each candidate set, given an assumed measurement error, and
  keeps a weight for every candidate.
- **Order.** Coefficients that set dates (phenology) are fitted first, against flowering and maturity dates; those
  that set weights (growth) after, against biomass and yield. Module 2's coefficient sweep shows why: the date
  coefficients move everything else, the growth ones do not move the dates.
- **Diverse data.** Experiments at several sites and sowing dates separate coefficients that would compensate for
  each other in one experiment: the day-length coefficients, for example, only show their effect across day
  lengths.


GLUE is one way to estimate cultivar coefficients. The course's lecture on estimating coefficients set it among
the others:

- **Measure the trait directly.** Controlled-environment experiments that control one or more factors (for
  example temperature or day length) and measure the crop's response.
- **Fit to field data**, the usual way: experiments with known weather, soil and management, and observed
  phenology, growth and yield. Within that:
  - **trial and error**: start from the closest cultivar in the DSSAT list, change one coefficient at a time,
    phenology first, and watch the error (module 4 gives the order);
  - **software-assisted search**: GenCalc, distributed with DSSAT, searches coefficients to minimize the error
    for chosen variables;
  - **Bayesian estimation**: GLUE, below, which also says how uncertain each value is.
- **Gene-based estimation**: coefficients expressed as functions of the alleles a cultivar carries, so they can be
  predicted from molecular markers. The course called this "in its infancy" in 2018.

Whatever the method, several sites and years estimate coefficients better than one: with one experiment, errors in
the weather, soil or measurements are absorbed into the coefficients.

### The observations

The course's GLUE exercise calibrates Williams-82, a soybean cultivar of maturity group 3, on the five treatments
it selects: the first treatment of four experiments from Ames, Iowa (IUAM) and Wooster, Ohio (OHWO), and the fully
irrigated treatment 4 of UFGA7902 from Gainesville, all shipped with DSSAT [@csmdata]. Dates are days after
planting.

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(gObs, {columns: ["exp", "ADAP", "MDAP", "HWAM", "CWAM", "PWAM", "LAIX", "HWUM"],
  header: {exp: "Experiment", ADAP: "Anthesis, DAP", MDAP: "Maturity, DAP", HWAM: "Seed yield, kg/ha", CWAM: "Tops, kg/ha", PWAM: "Pods, kg/ha", LAIX: "Max LAI", HWUM: "Seed size, g"},
  format: {HWUM: d => d?.toFixed(3)}, layout: "auto"})
```

Two more experiments, IUAM9701 and IUAM9702, are kept back to test the result; only their yield was
measured.

### Step 1: a range for every coefficient

GLUE draws candidate values uniformly within a range for each coefficient
([`Uniform.r`](https://github.com/DSSAT/glue/blob/e86093e400fbbdfc8e2c751c98acc2136835c3af/Uniform.r)).
DSSAT keeps the ranges in the cultivar file itself, in a `MINIMA` and a `MAXIMA` row, with a `!Calibration`
row that marks each coefficient as **P** (phenology), **G** (growth) or **N** (not calibrated).

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(gRanges, {columns: ["coef", "flag", "min", "max", "default", "outside_range"],
  header: {coef: "Coefficient", flag: "Flag", min: "MINIMA", max: "MAXIMA", default: "Williams-82 in the engine", outside_range: "Outside the range?"},
  format: {outside_range: v => v ? "yes" : ""}, layout: "auto", rows: 20})
```

```{ojs}
outside = gRanges.filter(d => d.outside_range === true && d.flag !== "N").map(d => d.coef)
// string literals stay in cells: Pandoc rewrites quotes and spaces inside inline expressions
outsideText = outside.join(" and ")
```

Note the last column: Williams-82's own values of ${outsideText} lie outside the ranges that GLUE samples from.

### Step 2: how likely is each candidate?

For every measurement, GLUE asks how likely the simulated value would be if the measurement had a normal
error with a fixed variance
([`Calculation.r`](https://github.com/DSSAT/glue/blob/e86093e400fbbdfc8e2c751c98acc2136835c3af/Calculation.r),
variances in
[`MeasurementVariance_All.csv`](https://github.com/DSSAT/glue/blob/e86093e400fbbdfc8e2c751c98acc2136835c3af/MeasurementVariance_All.csv)):
a standard deviation of 3 days for anthesis and 7 days for maturity, and 30% for yields and weights. The
likelihoods are multiplied over the measurements and the experiments and normalised, so the probabilities
of all candidates add up to 1. For candidate \(i\), measurement \(j\) with value \(O_j\), simulation \(S_{ij}\) and
variance \(\sigma_j^2\), in experiment \(e\):

\[
\begin{gathered}
L_{ij} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_j^2}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{(O_j - S_{ij})^2}{2\sigma_j^2}\right),
\qquad L_{ie} = \prod_{j \in e} L_{ij} \\[6pt]
p_i = \frac{\prod_e \left( L_{ie} \big/ \sum_k L_{ke} \right)}{\sum_m \prod_e \left( L_{me} \big/ \sum_k L_{ke} \right)}
\end{gathered}
\]

GLUE works in two rounds: round 1 varies the phenology coefficients and is
scored on the dates; round 2 keeps the best round-1 values and varies the growth coefficients, scored on
the weights. The notebook draws ${fmt.int(gInfo[0].sets_per_round)} candidates per round, ${fmt.int(gInfo[0].seasons)} soybean seasons in all.

Try the likelihood of one date: with a standard deviation of 3 days, how much less likely is a candidate that
misses anthesis by your chosen number of days than one that hits it?

```{ojs}
viewof miss = Inputs.range([0, 15], {step: 1, value: 4, label: "Days off"})
```

${missText}

```{ojs}
missText = miss === 0 ? "A candidate that hits the date has the highest likelihood; move the slider."
  : `${fmt.pct(Math.exp(-(miss ** 2) / 18))} as likely. Missing by ${2 * miss} days instead of ${miss} does not halve the likelihood: it divides it by ${fmt.int(Math.exp(-(miss ** 2) / 18) / Math.exp(-((2 * miss) ** 2) / 18))}.`
```

### Step 3: the posterior

Each dot is one candidate; its height is its GLUE probability.

```{ojs}
roundMap = new Map([["Round 1: phenology", gR1], ["Round 2: growth", gR2], ["Round 2, wider ranges", gR2w]])
viewof gRound = Inputs.radio([...roundMap.keys()], {value: "Round 1: phenology", label: "Round"})
```

```{ojs}
gSets = roundMap.get(gRound)
gCoefs = Object.keys(gSets[0]).filter(k => k !== "set" && k !== "prob")
viewof gCoef = Inputs.select(gCoefs, {label: "Coefficient"})
```

```{ojs}
postKey = gRound.startsWith("Round 1") ? "1" : gRound.includes("wider") ? "2, wider ranges" : "2"
gp = gPost.find(d => String(d.round) === postKey && d.coef === gCoef)
rg = gRanges.find(d => d.coef === gCoef)
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 320, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: gCoef, grid: true},
  y: {label: "GLUE probability", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([gp], {x1: "prior_min", x2: "prior_max", fill: "#c4a35a", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.dot(gSets, {x: gCoef, y: "prob", r: 1.6, fill: "#2a7f62", fillOpacity: 0.5, tip: true}),
    Plot.ruleX([rg.default], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([gp.best], {stroke: "#d9822b", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.text([{x: rg.default, t: "Williams-82 in the engine"}, {x: gp.best, t: "best"}], {x: "x", text: "t", frameAnchor: "top", dy: 6, dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#555"})
  ]
}), `module3-glue-${postKey}-${gCoef}`)
```

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(gPost.filter(d => String(d.round) === postKey), {columns: ["coef", "best", "mean", "sd", "prior_min", "prior_max"],
  header: {coef: "Coefficient", best: "Most probable set", mean: "Posterior mean", sd: "Posterior sd", prior_min: "Range from", prior_max: "to"},
  format: {best: d => d.toPrecision(4), mean: d => d.toPrecision(4), sd: d => d.toPrecision(2)}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
nNear = (sets) => sets.filter(d => d.prob > d3.max(sets, s => s.prob) / 100).length
```

Many candidates are almost as good as the best. In round 1, ${nNear(gR1)} of the ${fmt.int(gR1.length)} candidates have
at least 1% of the best candidate's probability; in round 2, ${nNear(gR2)}. Different combinations of
coefficients reproduce the same observations (*equifinality*). That is why the posterior mean and spread
matter as much as the single best set.

### When the best value sits on the edge

If the best value of a coefficient lies at the edge of its range, the data want a value the range does not
allow. That happens in round 2. The notebook reruns round 2 with those ranges widened by half their width
on the side that was hit:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(gWide, {header: {coef: "Coefficient", best: "Best in round 2", side: "Edge", old_min: "Range from", old_max: "to", new_min: "Wider from", new_max: "to"},
  format: {best: d => d.toPrecision(4)}, layout: "auto"})
```

### Result: better dates; the weights depend on the ranges

```{ojs}
viewof eVar = Inputs.select(new Map([["Anthesis, DAP", "ADAP"], ["Maturity, DAP", "MDAP"], ["Seed yield, kg/ha", "HWAM"], ["Tops, kg/ha", "CWAM"], ["Pods, kg/ha", "PWAM"], ["Max LAI", "LAIX"], ["Seed size, g", "HWUM"]]), {value: "MDAP", label: "Variable"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = gEval.filter(d => d.variable === eVar);
  const ext = d3.extent(rows.flatMap(d => [d.simulated, d.observed]));
  const pad = (ext[1] - ext[0]) * 0.1 || 1, lo = ext[0] - pad, hi = ext[1] + pad;
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: Math.min(W, 520), height: 420, marginLeft: 60,
    x: {label: `Observed`, domain: [lo, hi], grid: true},
    y: {label: `Simulated`, domain: [lo, hi], grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: versions, range: vColors},
    symbol: {legend: true, domain: ["calibration", "independent check"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.line([[lo, lo], [hi, hi]], {stroke: "#bbb", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "observed", y: "simulated", stroke: "version", symbol: "use", r: 6, strokeWidth: 2, tip: true, channels: {experiment: "exp"}})
    ]
  }), `module3-glue-eval-${eVar}`);
}
```

```{ojs}
statTab = [...new Set(gStats.map(d => d.variable))].map(v => {
  const o = {variable: v};
  for (const ver of versions) { const r = gStats.find(d => d.variable === v && d.version === ver); o[ver] = r?.rmse; o[`d ${ver}`] = r?.d; }
  return o;
})
Inputs.table(statTab, {columns: ["variable", ...versions], header: {variable: "Variable (calibration experiments)", default: "RMSE, default", GLUE: "RMSE, GLUE", "GLUE, wider ranges": "RMSE, GLUE wider"},
  format: Object.fromEntries(versions.map(v => [v, d => d < 1 ? d.toFixed(3) : d < 20 ? d.toFixed(1) : fmt.int(d)])), layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
st = (v, ver) => gStats.find(d => d.variable === v && d.version === ver).rmse
calE = gEval.filter(d => d.use === "calibration")
cmpE = (v) => [...new Set(calE.map(d => d.exp))].map(e => ({e, g: calE.find(d => d.exp === e && d.variable === v && d.version === "GLUE")?.simulated,
  d0: calE.find(d => d.exp === e && d.variable === v && d.version === "default")?.simulated})).filter(d => d.g != null && d.d0 != null)
calN = cmpE("MDAP").length
laterN = cmpE("MDAP").filter(d => d.g > d.d0).length
moreTopsN = cmpE("CWAM").filter(d => d.g > d.d0).length
```

GLUE improves the dates: the error in anthesis falls from ${fmt.d1(st("ADAP", "default"))} to ${fmt.d1(st("ADAP", "GLUE"))} days and in maturity from ${fmt.d1(st("MDAP", "default"))} to ${fmt.d1(st("MDAP", "GLUE"))} days. It does not improve the weights. The default Williams-82 reproduces tops weight with an error of ${fmt.int(st("CWAM", "default"))} kg/ha, the GLUE cultivar with ${fmt.int(st("CWAM", "GLUE"))},
and with the wider ranges ${fmt.int(st("CWAM", "GLUE, wider ranges"))}. Two things on this page point to why. The new
phenology lengthens the season (later maturity in ${laterN} of ${calN} experiments), and the GLUE cultivar grows more
tops in ${moreTopsN} of them. And the growth coefficients that could offset that, the leaf photosynthesis rate `LFMAX`
among them, were sampled inside ranges that exclude the engine's own Williams-82 values. A calibration is only as good as its observations, its ranges
and its error model; GLUE makes all three explicit, which is its main use.


### GLUE self test 4: a new maize hybrid from Colorado

The course's last GLUE exercise calibrates a cultivar DSSAT does not have yet: the maize hybrid DEKALB 52-59 AF,
grown at Greeley, Colorado, in 2008 and 2010 under full irrigation and with 40% of it [@anothai2013]. The
experiment files, weather and soils came with the course. The exercise asks for a new cultivar entry, `CO0801`,
built from an existing variety; the notebook starts from DEKALB 485 (`IB1072`) of the engine's cultivar file and
runs both GLUE rounds on all four treatments.

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(coPost, {columns: ["round", "coef", "DEKALB 485", "best", "mean", "sd", "prior_min", "prior_max"],
  header: {round: "Round", coef: "Coefficient", best: "CO0801 (most probable)", mean: "Posterior mean", sd: "Posterior sd", prior_min: "Range from", prior_max: "to"},
  format: {best: d => d.toPrecision(4), mean: d => d.toPrecision(4), sd: d => d.toPrecision(2), prior_min: d => d.toPrecision(3), prior_max: d => d.toPrecision(3)}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof coVar = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Anthesis, DAP", "ADAP"], ["Maturity, DAP", "MDAP"], ["Grain yield, kg/ha", "HWAM"], ["Tops, kg/ha", "CWAM"]]), {value: "ADAP", label: "Variable"})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 300, marginLeft: 110, marginRight: 20,
  x: {label: coVar, grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["DEKALB 485 as it is", "GLUE: CO0801", "observed"], range: ["#999999", "#3f7a34", "#f2a33a"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(coEval.filter(d => d.variable === coVar), {y: "exp", x: "simulated", fill: "version", r: 6, tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(coEval.filter(d => d.variable === coVar && d.version === "GLUE: CO0801"), {y: "exp", x: "observed", fill: () => "observed", symbol: "diamond", r: 7, tip: true})
  ]
}), `module3-colorado-${coVar}`)
```

```{ojs}
coRmse = (v, ver) => Math.sqrt(d3.mean(coEval.filter(d => d.variable === v && d.version === ver), d => (d.simulated - d.observed) ** 2))
```

The phenology moves most: the anthesis error falls from ${fmt.d1(coRmse("ADAP", "DEKALB 485 as it is"))} to ${fmt.d1(coRmse("ADAP", "GLUE: CO0801"))} days. Grain yield goes from an error of ${fmt.int(coRmse("HWAM", "DEKALB 485 as it is"))} to ${fmt.int(coRmse("HWAM", "GLUE: CO0801"))} kg/ha over the four treatments. With two years and two irrigation levels, four observations of each
variable carry the whole calibration; the posterior spread above shows how loosely that pins the growth
coefficients down.

### Calibration with in-season data: peanut UFGA8401

The second calibration exercise of the course works by hand, against growth analysis data taken during the season:
the irrigated treatment of the 1984 Florunner peanut experiment UFGA8401. It asks for four statistics of four
variables, tops weight, seed weight, seed number and pod harvest index: the RMSE, the intercept `a` and slope `b`
of the regression of simulated on observed values (a good fit has `a` near 0 and `b` near 1), and Willmott's `d`.
It suggests four coefficients: `LFMAX` for the size of tops and seed weight, `FL-SH` and `FL-SD` moved together
for the timing of seed growth, `PODUR` for the first rise of seed number and pod harvest index, and `XFRT` for the
share of growth that goes to pods and seeds.

The notebook runs every combination of five values of `LFMAX`, five shifts of `FL-SH` and `FL-SD`, five values
of `PODUR` and the values of `XFRT`, so you can move them here freely.

```{ojs}
pi0 = pnInfo[0]
lfV = [...new Set(pnGrid.map(d => d.LFMAX))].sort(d3.ascending)
shV = [...new Set(pnGrid.map(d => d.shift))].sort(d3.ascending)
poV = [...new Set(pnGrid.map(d => d.PODUR))].sort(d3.ascending)
xfV = [...new Set(pnGrid.map(d => d.XFRT))].sort(d3.ascending)
viewof pLf = Inputs.range([0, lfV.length - 1], {step: 1, value: lfV.indexOf(pi0.LFMAX), label: "LFMAX", format: i => lfV[i]})
viewof pSh = Inputs.range([0, shV.length - 1], {step: 1, value: shV.indexOf(0), label: "FL-SH, FL-SD shift, days", format: i => shV[i]})
viewof pPo = Inputs.range([0, poV.length - 1], {step: 1, value: poV.indexOf(pi0.PODUR), label: "PODUR", format: i => poV[i]})
viewof pXf = Inputs.range([0, xfV.length - 1], {step: 1, value: xfV.indexOf(pi0.XFRT), label: "XFRT", format: i => xfV[i]})
viewof pVar = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Tops weight", "CWAD"], ["Seed weight", "GWAD"], ["Seed number", "G#AD"], ["Pod harvest index", "HIPD"]]), {value: "GWAD", label: "Variable"})
```

```{ojs}
pSet = pnGrid.find(d => d.LFMAX === lfV[pLf] && d.shift === shV[pSh] && d.PODUR === poV[pPo] && d.XFRT === xfV[pXf]).set
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 330, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: pVar, grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Florunner as it is", "your coefficients", "observed"], range: ["#999999", "#3f7a34", "#f2a33a"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(pnDaily.filter(d => d.set === pi0.base_set), {x: "DAP", y: pVar, stroke: () => "Florunner as it is", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(pnDaily.filter(d => d.set === pSet), {x: "DAP", y: pVar, stroke: () => "your coefficients", strokeWidth: 2.5, tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(pnObs.filter(d => d[pVar] != null), {x: "DAP", y: pVar, fill: () => "observed", r: 4, tip: true})
  ]
}), `module3-peanut-${pVar.replace(/[^A-Z]/gi, "")}`)
```

```{ojs}
pTab = ["CWAD", "GWAD", "G#AD", "HIPD"].map(v => {
  const a = pnStats.find(d => d.set === pi0.base_set && d.variable === v), b = pnStats.find(d => d.set === pSet && d.variable === v);
  return {variable: ({CWAD: "Tops weight", GWAD: "Seed weight", "G#AD": "Seed number", HIPD: "Pod harvest index"})[v],
          rmse0: a.rmse, rmse: b.rmse, a: b.a, b: b.b, d0: a.d, d: b.d};
})
Inputs.table(pTab, {header: {variable: "Variable", rmse0: "RMSE, Florunner", rmse: "RMSE, yours", a: "a, yours", b: "b, yours", d0: "d, Florunner", d: "d, yours"},
  format: {rmse0: d => d < 1 ? d.toFixed(3) : fmt.int(d), rmse: d => d < 1 ? d.toFixed(3) : fmt.int(d), a: d => Math.abs(d) < 1 ? d.toFixed(3) : fmt.int(d),
           b: d => d.toFixed(2), d0: d => d.toFixed(3), d: d => d.toFixed(3)}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
pBest = pnGrid.find(d => d.set === pi0.best_set)
meanD = (set) => d3.mean(pnStats.filter(d => d.set === set), d => d.d)
```

Of all ${pnGrid.length} combinations, the one with the highest mean `d` over the four variables has `LFMAX` ${pBest.LFMAX}, a shift of ${pBest.shift} days, `PODUR` ${pBest.PODUR} and `XFRT` ${pBest.XFRT} (mean d ${meanD(pi0.best_set).toFixed(3)}, against ${meanD(pi0.base_set).toFixed(3)} for Florunner as it is). The course's self test asks for a second pass
through the coefficients starting from the improved cultivar; the sliders let you do that pass here.

## 2. Soil data

A DSSAT soil profile lists layers with their lower limit of plant-extractable water (`SLLL`, close to the
wilting point), drained upper limit (`SDUL`, close to field capacity), saturation (`SSAT`), a root growth
factor (`SRGF`), texture and organic carbon. The water a soil can store for a crop is the sum over the
layers,

\[
PAW = \sum_{l} \left(DUL_l - LL_l\right)\,\Delta z_l ,
\]

with \(\Delta z_l\) the thickness of layer \(l\) (in mm for PAW in mm).

```{ojs}
viewof soilId = Inputs.select(soilPaw.map(d => d.id), {value: "IBMZ910014", label: "Profile", format: id => soilPaw.find(d => d.id === id).name})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const lay = soilLayers.filter(d => d.id === soilId);
  const long = lay.flatMap(d => [["LL", "lower limit (SLLL)"], ["DUL", "drained upper limit (SDUL)"], ["SAT", "saturation (SSAT)"]]
    .flatMap(([k, n]) => [{depth: d.top, v: d[k], what: n}, {depth: d.bottom, v: d[k], what: n}]));
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: Math.min(W, 520), height: 380, marginLeft: 55,
    x: {label: "Volumetric water content, cm³/cm³", domain: [0, 0.6], grid: true},
    y: {label: "Depth, cm", reverse: true, grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["lower limit (SLLL)", "drained upper limit (SDUL)", "saturation (SSAT)"], range: ["#d9822b", "#2a7f62", "#4a6fa5"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaX(lay.flatMap(d => [{depth: d.top, a: d.LL, b: d.DUL}, {depth: d.bottom, a: d.LL, b: d.DUL}]), {y: "depth", x1: "a", x2: "b", fill: "#2a7f62", fillOpacity: 0.15}),
      Plot.line(long, {x: "v", y: "depth", stroke: "what", strokeWidth: 2, tip: true})
    ]
  }), `module3-soil-${soilId}`);
}
```

The shaded band is the plant-available water. Across the thirteen profiles:

### Estimating water limits from texture

When only texture and organic matter are known, a pedotransfer function estimates the limits. xdssat uses
the equations of Saxton and Rawls [-@saxton2006] (`src/soils.py`), ported below; for the lower limit, with
sand \(S\), clay \(C\) as fractions and organic matter \(OM\) in %:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta_{1500t} &= -0.024S + 0.487C + 0.006\,OM \\
&\quad + 0.005\,S\,OM - 0.013\,C\,OM + 0.068\,S\,C + 0.031 \\
LL &= \theta_{1500t} + (0.14\,\theta_{1500t} - 0.02)
\end{aligned}
\]

and similar equations for the drained upper limit and saturation; DSSAT's SBuild tool has its
own. Move the sliders:

```{ojs}
viewof srSand = Inputs.range([0, 95], {step: 1, value: 60, label: "Sand, %"})
viewof srClay = Inputs.range([0, 60], {step: 1, value: 15, label: "Clay, %"})
viewof srOM = Inputs.range([0, 8], {step: 0.1, value: 1.5, label: "Organic matter, %"})
```

```{ojs}
function saxtonRawls(sand, clay, om) {
  const S = sand, C = clay, OM = om;
  const t1500 = -0.024 * S + 0.487 * C + 0.006 * OM + 0.005 * S * OM - 0.013 * C * OM + 0.068 * S * C + 0.031;
  const ll = t1500 + (0.14 * t1500 - 0.02);
  const t33 = -0.251 * S + 0.195 * C + 0.011 * OM + 0.006 * S * OM - 0.027 * C * OM + 0.452 * S * C + 0.299;
  const dul = t33 + (1.283 * t33 ** 2 - 0.374 * t33 - 0.015);
  const ts33 = 0.278 * S + 0.034 * C + 0.022 * OM - 0.018 * S * OM - 0.027 * C * OM - 0.584 * S * C + 0.078;
  const s33 = ts33 + (0.636 * ts33 - 0.107);
  return {ll, dul, sat: dul + s33 - 0.097 * S + 0.043};
}
srOut = srSand + srClay > 100 ? null : saxtonRawls(srSand / 100, srClay / 100, srOM)
```

${srText}

```{ojs}
srText = srOut ? `LL ${srOut.ll.toFixed(3)}, DUL ${srOut.dul.toFixed(3)}, SAT ${srOut.sat.toFixed(3)} cm³/cm³: ${fmt.int((srOut.dul - srOut.ll) * 1000)} mm of available water per metre of such soil.` : "Sand and clay add up to more than 100%."
```

Applied to the layers of the soil file, the estimates miss the file's values by a root mean square of ${srRmse.LL} (LL), ${srRmse.DUL} (DUL) and ${srRmse.SAT} (SAT) cm³/cm³. The file's generic profiles were not made with this
function, so the comparison shows how much two reasonable estimates can differ, not which one is right.

```{ojs}
srRmse = Object.fromEntries(["LL", "DUL", "SAT"].map(k => [k, Math.sqrt(d3.mean(soilSR, d => (d[k] - d[k + "_sr"]) ** 2)).toFixed(3)]))
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 520), height: 380, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "In the soil file, cm³/cm³", domain: [0, 0.6], grid: true},
  y: {label: "Saxton and Rawls, cm³/cm³", domain: [0, 0.6], grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["LL", "DUL", "SAT"], range: ["#d9822b", "#2a7f62", "#4a6fa5"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([[0, 0], [0.6, 0.6]], {stroke: "#bbb", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    ...["LL", "DUL", "SAT"].map(k => Plot.dot(soilSR, {x: k, y: k + "_sr", stroke: () => k, r: 3, tip: true, channels: {profile: "name", "bottom, cm": "bottom"}}))
  ]
}), "module3-saxton-rawls")
```

The soil exercise gives the laboratory sheets of two soil series and asks for a DSSAT profile of each, with the

A sheet can be wrong. In the Umariya sheet the 11-31 cm layer has 55.2% sand, 18.4% silt and 36.4% clay, which

Saxton and Rawls use sand and clay only, so the notebook keeps both as printed. Had the sand been 45.2% (the value

**Self test 3** compares Orangeburg's estimated limits with the water contents the sheet measured at 1/3 bar
(33 kPa) and 15 bar (1500 kPa). The sheet gives them in % by weight; times bulk density they are volumetric. Its

Inputs.table(soilOg, {columns: ["horizon", "top", "bottom", "clay", "DUL_measured", "DUL_sr", "LL_measured", "LL_sr", "available_check", "available_water_fc"],

The pedotransfer function puts the drained upper limit ${ogBias > 0 ? "above" : "below"} the measured 1/3 bar water by ${Math.abs(ogBias).toFixed(3)} cm³/cm³ on average, and the lower limit ${ogBiasLL > 0 ? "above" : "below"} the 15 bar water by ${Math.abs(ogBiasLL).toFixed(3)}. Where a soil was measured, measured limits beat estimated ones; the soil file
already holds an Orangeburg sandy loam (`IBSB910017`), shown in the selector above for comparison (self test 2).

## 3. Water-limited production

The course's water-limited exercise builds `UFGA8212.MZX` from the potential production experiment of module 1:
McCurdy 84aa maize planted on 26 February 1982 (7.2 plants/m², 61 cm rows, 7 cm deep), the Millhopper fine
sand, simulation from 25 February with the initial soil water the exercise lists, the water balance on and
nitrogen off. Treatment 1 is **rainfed** (no irrigation at all); treatment 2 irrigates **automatically** when the
available water in the top 30 cm falls below 50%. Rain and irrigation enter the soil; water runs off, drains below
the profile, evaporates from the soil surface and is taken up by roots from each layer
([`WATBAL.for`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Soil/SoilWater/WATBAL.for)).
Self test 1 adds potential production for comparison.


**Creating the FileX: the water balance on.** Two parts of the experiment file change from module 1. The
treatment table gives the rainfed treatment irrigation level 0 (`MI`), and the simulation controls switch the
water balance on (`WATER` = `Y`) and, for the irrigated treatment, irrigation to automatic (`IRRIG` = `A`, with
the depth `IMDEP` and threshold `ITHRL` in the automatic management rows). The rainfed file:

### Runoff and water stress, as the engine computes them

The soil water of the profile changes each day by what comes in and what goes out:

\[
\Delta SW = P + I - R - D - E_s - E_p
\]

(rain, irrigation, runoff, drainage, soil evaporation, transpiration). Two of the terms in a few lines each.
**Runoff** uses the curve number method of the US Soil Conservation Service: with the soil's curve number \(CN\)
and the day's water \(P\) (mm),

\[
\begin{gathered}
S = 254\left(\frac{100}{CN} - 1\right) \\[4pt]
R = \begin{cases} \dfrac{(P - I_a S)^2}{P + (1 - I_a)\,S} & P > I_a S \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{gathered}
\]

with \(I_a\) the initial abstraction
([`RNOFF.for:78-105`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Soil/SoilWater/RNOFF.for#L78)). The engine sets `Ia` from how wet the top two layers are
(lines 84-86): about 0.3 when they are dry, near 0 when they are saturated.

```{ojs}
viewof cn = Inputs.range([50, 95], {step: 1, value: 60, label: "Curve number CN"})
viewof ia = Inputs.range([0, 0.3], {step: 0.01, value: 0.15, label: "Initial abstraction Ia"})
```

```{ojs}
runoff = (p, cn, ia) => { const S = 254 * (100 / cn - 1); const pb = p - ia * S; return pb > 0 ? pb ** 2 / (p + (1 - ia) * S) : 0; }
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 600), height: 280, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Rain on the day, mm", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Runoff, mm", grid: true},
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([0]), Plot.lineY(d3.range(0, 151, 1).map(p => ({p, r: runoff(p, cn, ia)})), {x: "p", y: "r", stroke: "#4a6fa5", strokeWidth: 2.5, tip: true})]
}), `module3-runoff-cn${cn}`)
```

With CN ${cn}, a 60 mm storm runs off ${fmt.d1(runoff(60, cn, ia))} mm. A soil profile carries its curve number as `SLRO`: 60 for the Millhopper fine sand, which is where the slider starts.

**Water stress.** Each day the engine compares what the roots can take up (`TRWUP`) with what the crop could
transpire (`EP1`). CERES-Maize turns the ratio into two factors
([`MZ_GROSUB.for:1065-1076`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CERES-Maize/MZ_GROSUB.for#L1065)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
SWFAC &= \min\!\left(1, \frac{TRWUP}{EP_1}\right) && \text{(photosynthesis)} \\[4pt]
TURFAC &= \min\!\left(1, \frac{TRWUP}{RWUEP1 \cdot EP_1}\right) && \text{(leaf expansion)}
\end{aligned}
\]

with `RWUEP1` = 1.5 in the maize species file. Expansion is hit first, while the supply
still covers the demand:

```{ojs}
viewof supply = Inputs.range([0, 2.5], {step: 0.05, value: 1.2, label: "Root supply / transpiration demand"})
```

```{ojs}
sw = (r) => Math.min(1, r)
tu = (r) => Math.min(1, r / 1.5)
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 600), height: 260, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Root supply / transpiration demand", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Factor (1 = no stress)", domain: [0, 1.05], grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["SWFAC (photosynthesis)", "TURFAC (expansion)"], range: ["#f2a33a", "#3f7a34"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(d3.range(0, 2.51, 0.01).map(r => ({r, v: sw(r), k: "SWFAC (photosynthesis)"})), {x: "r", y: "v", stroke: "k", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.lineY(d3.range(0, 2.51, 0.01).map(r => ({r, v: tu(r), k: "TURFAC (expansion)"})), {x: "r", y: "v", stroke: "k", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([supply], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
  ]
}), "module3-water-stress-factors")
```

At a ratio of ${supply}: SWFAC ${sw(supply).toFixed(2)}, TURFAC ${tu(supply).toFixed(2)}.

### Soil water, layer by layer

The fill is the plant-available water of each layer: 0 at the lower limit, 1 at the drained upper limit (above 1
the layer holds more than it can keep against drainage). Depths are those the engine simulates, which differ from
the layers of the soil file: the engine keeps 5 and 15 cm at the top and splits thick layers
([`LYRSET2`, `LMATCH.for:263`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Soil/SoilUtilities/LMATCH.for#L263),
ported as `learnlib.engine_layers`).

```{ojs}
viewof swLev = Inputs.radio(["rainfed", "automatic irrigation"], {value: "rainfed", label: "Treatment"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const lay = new Map(wlLayers.map(d => [d.layer, d]));
  const rows = wlSW.filter(d => d.level === swLev && lay.has(d.layer)).map(d => {
    const L = lay.get(d.layer); return {...d, top: L.top, bottom: L.bottom, rel: (d.SW - L.LL) / (L.DUL - L.LL)};
  });
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: W, height: 330, marginLeft: 55,
    x: {label: "Days after the start of the simulation"},
    y: {label: "Depth, cm", reverse: true},
    color: {type: "linear", domain: [0, 1.2], range: ["#b5651d", "#f3e9c6", "#3f7a34"], interpolate: "rgb", legend: true, label: "Relative available water"},
    marks: [Plot.rect(rows, {x1: "DAS", x2: d => d.DAS + 1, y1: "top", y2: "bottom", fill: "rel", tip: true, channels: {"SW, cm³/cm³": "SW"}})]
  }), `module3-soil-water-${swLev.replace(" ", "-")}`);
}
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 280, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Water stress index (0 = none)", domain: [0, 1], grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["rainfed", "automatic irrigation"], range: ["#f2a33a", "#3f7a34"]},
  marks: [Plot.lineY(wlBal.filter(d => d.DAP >= 0), {x: "DAP", y: "WSGD", stroke: "level", tip: true})]
}), "module3-water-stress")
```

::: {.source-note}
Water stress index: `WSGD` of PlantGro, the expansion and partitioning stress written as 1 minus the factor
([`MZ_OPGROW.for:175`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CERES-Maize/MZ_OPGROW.for#L175)).

### Self test 2: which soil holds the most water for the crop?

The rainfed treatment on the twelve generic profiles, the Millhopper fine sand, and the two profiles built from
the course's soil sheets, each starting at 100% of its plant-available water:

```{ojs}
srcColor = new Map([["SOIL.SOL", "#3f7a34"], ["course exercise", "#f2a33a"]])
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 660), height: 380, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Plant-available water of the profile, mm", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Rainfed grain yield, kg/ha", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["SOIL.SOL", "course exercise"], range: ["#3f7a34", "#f2a33a"]},
  symbol: {legend: true, domain: [60, 150, 180, 210], tickFormat: d => `${d} cm deep`},
  marks: [Plot.dot(wlSoils, {x: "paw_mm", y: "HWAM", stroke: "source", symbol: d => d.depth_cm, r: 6, strokeWidth: 2, tip: true,
    channels: {soil: "name", "drainage, mm": "DRCM", "runoff, mm": "ROCM"}})]
}), "module3-yield-vs-paw")
```

```{ojs}
rPaw = (() => { const x = wlSoils.map(d => d.paw_mm), y = wlSoils.map(d => d.HWAM); const mx = d3.mean(x), my = d3.mean(y);
  return d3.sum(x, (v, i) => (v - mx) * (y[i] - my)) / Math.sqrt(d3.sum(x, v => (v - mx) ** 2) * d3.sum(y, v => (v - my) ** 2)); })()
mill = wlSoils.find(d => d.id === "IBMZ910014")
lessStore = wlSoils.filter(d => d.paw_mm < mill.paw_mm && d.HWAM > mill.HWAM).length
bestSoil = wlSoils.reduce((a, b) => b.HWAM > a.HWAM ? b : a)
```

Yield rises with the soil's storage (r = ${rPaw.toFixed(2)} over the ${wlSoils.length} soils). Closest to potential production comes the ${bestSoil.name.toLowerCase()}, with ${fmt.int(bestSoil.HWAM)} kg/ha. Storage is not the only property that counts: the Millhopper fine sand stores ${fmt.int(mill.paw_mm)} mm and yields ${fmt.int(mill.HWAM)} kg/ha, less than ${lessStore} soils that store less water, and it loses ${fmt.int(mill.DRCM)} mm to drainage against a median of ${fmt.int(d3.median(wlSoils, d => d.DRCM))} mm.

### Self test 3: when to irrigate

With `IRRIG` = `A` the engine irrigates when the available water in the top `IMDEP` cm falls to `ITHRL` percent of
its capacity, and refills it to `ITHRU`
([`IRRIG.for:827`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Management/IRRIG.for#L827)).
The exercise's grid of management depths and thresholds:

```{ojs}
viewof aVar = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Grain yield, kg/ha", "HWAM"], ["Irrigation, mm", "IRCM"], ["Number of irrigations", "irrigations"], ["Extra grain per mm of irrigation", "kg_grain_per_mm_irrigation"]]), {value: "HWAM", label: "Show"})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 560), height: 300, marginLeft: 70, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {label: "Threshold ITHRL, % of available water", type: "band"},
  y: {label: "Management depth IMDEP, cm", type: "band"},
  color: {scheme: "YlGn", legend: true, label: aVar},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(wlAuto, {x: "threshold", y: "depth_cm", fill: aVar, inset: 1, tip: true, channels: {"yield, kg/ha": "HWAM", "irrigation, mm": "IRCM", irrigations: "irrigations"}}),
    Plot.text(wlAuto, {x: "threshold", y: "depth_cm", text: d => d[aVar] == null ? "" : d[aVar] < 100 ? d[aVar].toFixed(aVar === "irrigations" ? 0 : 1) : fmt.int(d[aVar]), fill: "#222", fontSize: 10})
  ]
}), `module3-auto-irrigation-${aVar}`)
```

```{ojs}
fullY = d3.max(wlAuto, d => d.HWAM)
cheapest = wlAuto.filter(d => d.HWAM >= fullY - 0.5).reduce((a, b) => b.IRCM < a.IRCM ? b : a)
aEff = wlAuto.reduce((a, b) => (b.kg_grain_per_mm_irrigation ?? -1) > (a.kg_grain_per_mm_irrigation ?? -1) ? b : a)
```

The full yield of ${fmt.int(fullY)} kg/ha needs least water at ${cheapest.depth_cm} cm and ${cheapest.threshold}%: ${fmt.int(cheapest.IRCM)} mm in ${cheapest.irrigations} applications. The most grain per mm of irrigation comes at ${aEff.depth_cm} cm and ${aEff.threshold}%, a lower yield (${fmt.int(aEff.HWAM)} kg/ha): the best setting depends on whether water or land is the scarcer resource.

### Self test 4: other years at Gainesville

The rainfed and automatically irrigated maize planted on 26 February of every year with a full Gainesville
weather file in dssat-csm-data:

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 320, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Grain yield, kg/ha", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["rainfed", "automatic irrigation"], range: ["#f2a33a", "#3f7a34"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(wlYears.filter(d => d.level === "rainfed"), {x: "year", y1: d => d.HWAM, y2: d => wlYears.find(e => e.year === d.year && e.level !== "rainfed").HWAM, stroke: "#ddd"}),
    Plot.dot(wlYears, {x: "year", y: "HWAM", fill: "level", r: 5, tip: true, channels: {"rain, mm": "PRCM", "irrigation, mm": "IRCM"}})
  ]
}), "module3-gainesville-years")
```

```{ojs}
yrR = wlYears.filter(d => d.level === "rainfed")
yrI = wlYears.filter(d => d.level !== "rainfed")
```

Over ${yrR.length} years the rainfed yield ranges from ${fmt.int(d3.min(yrR, d => d.HWAM))} to ${fmt.int(d3.max(yrR, d => d.HWAM))} kg/ha, the irrigated one only from ${fmt.int(d3.min(yrI, d => d.HWAM))} to ${fmt.int(d3.max(yrI, d => d.HWAM))}: irrigation removes most of the year-to-year variation, and what remains comes from the rest of the weather.

### Paddy rice: the flood water balance

In bunded, puddled rice fields the water balance has one more store: the flood above the soil. Bunds hold rain and irrigation as standing water up to their height. The flood loses water by evaporation,
by infiltration into the puddled soil at a percolation rate, and by spilling over the bund when it rises above
it. The engine keeps this balance every day when the irrigation section of the experiment file sets the paddy
operations, and writes it to `FloodW.OUT`
([`Management/OpFlood.for`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Management/OpFlood.for)). The operations are codes of the engine's
`DETAIL.CDE`: `IR010` puddling, `IR008` percolation rate (mm/day), `IR009` bund height (mm), `IR011` constant
flood depth (mm) and `IR006` flood depth (mm).

The runs use xdssat's own rice template, `templates/XDRI8601.RIX`: IRRI's IR 58 experiment at Munoz,
Philippines (IRMZ8601), with an added rainfed bunded water level. Its three water regimes, in the irrigation
section below, are run in the dry season as in the experiment (transplanted early February 1986) and in the wet
season (1 July 1986), with nitrogen off so that only water differs.

```{ojs}
flSum = FileAttachment("data/module3/flood_summary.csv").csv({typed: true})
flDaily = FileAttachment("data/module3/flood_daily.csv").csv({typed: true})
flFiles = FileAttachment("data/module3/flood_files.csv").csv()
html`<pre class="filex">${flFiles[0].text}</pre>`
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 380, marginLeft: 55, marginRight: 90,
  x: {label: "Days after the start of the simulation", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Flood depth, mm", grid: true},
  fy: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["flooded, 50 mm kept", "flooded, drained twice", "rainfed, bunded"], range: ["#2a6f97", "#7fb3d5", "#f2a33a"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(flDaily, {x: "DAS", y: "ABUND", fy: "season", stroke: "#bbb", strokeDasharray: "3,3", z: "regime"}),
    Plot.lineY(flDaily, {x: "DAS", y: "FLOD", fy: "season", stroke: "regime", tip: true, channels: {"rain, mm": "PRED", "irrigation, mm": "IRRD", "over the bund, mm": "FROD"}})
  ]
}), "module3-paddy-flood-depth")
```

Lines: flood depth; dashed grey: bund height.

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(flSum, {columns: ["season", "regime", "HWAM", "days_to_maturity", "PRCM", "IRCM", "flood_days", "flood_evap", "infiltration", "over_bund", "WSPD"],
  header: {season: "Season", regime: "Water regime", HWAM: "Grain, kg/ha", days_to_maturity: "Days to maturity", PRCM: "Rain, mm", IRCM: "Irrigation, mm",
           flood_days: "Days with flood", flood_evap: "Evaporation from flood, mm", infiltration: "Infiltration, mm", over_bund: "Over the bund, mm", WSPD: "Mean water stress (photosynthesis)"},
  format: {WSPD: d => d.toFixed(2), flood_evap: d => d.toFixed(0), infiltration: d => d.toFixed(0), over_bund: d => d.toFixed(0)}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
flPick = (season, regime) => flSum.find(d => d.season === season && d.regime === regime)
flWet = flSum.filter(d => d.season === "wet season")
flDryF = flPick("dry season", "flooded, 50 mm kept")
flDryR = flPick("dry season", "rainfed, bunded")
flWetR = flPick("wet season", "rainfed, bunded")
flWetSpread = d3.max(flWet, d => d.HWAM) - d3.min(flWet, d => d.HWAM)
flWetYield = flWetSpread === 0 ? "the same grain yield, " + fmt.int(flWet[0].HWAM) + " kg/ha" : "grain yields within " + fmt.int(flWetSpread) + " kg/ha of each other"
flDryLoss = flDryF.HWAM - flDryR.HWAM
```

In the wet season the bunds alone keep the field flooded: the rainfed field has standing water on ${flWetR.flood_days} days without any irrigation, ${fmt.int(flWetR.over_bund)} mm of rain spills over its bund, and the three regimes give ${flWetYield}. In the dry season the rainfed field has a flood on ${flDryR.flood_days} day and its crop is water-stressed (mean stress factor ${flDryR.WSPD.toFixed(2)}, against ${flDryF.WSPD.toFixed(2)} when flooded). In these runs the stressed crop takes ${flDryR.days_to_maturity} days from planting to maturity against ${flDryF.days_to_maturity}; over that longer season it receives ${fmt.int(flDryR.PRCM)} mm of rain against ${fmt.int(flDryF.PRCM)} mm, because the 1986 rains at Munoz start in May, and its simulated yield is ${fmt.int(flDryLoss)} kg/ha below the flooded crop's. Kept flooded, the dry-season crop receives ${fmt.int(flDryF.IRCM)} mm of irrigation, and ${fmt.int(flDryF.infiltration)} mm of water infiltrates from the flood into the puddled soil. These runs change only the water regime: to see how much the bund height (`IR009`) and the percolation rate (`IR008`) matter, change them in the notebook and rerun.

## From one field to a grid: xdssat

Section 2 built two soil profiles by hand. For a region, xdssat builds one per cell: texture and organic carbon
from SoilGrids [@poggio2021] at six depths, water limits from `soils.saxton_rawls`, the same function used above,
and the root growth factor from `soils.root_growth_factor`. The plant-available water of the profiles of the
[rice case study](../java/index.qmd):

```{ojs}
import {cellFeatures, adminMarks} from "../assets/js/dl.js"
gCells = FileAttachment("../java/data/grid_cells.csv").csv({typed: true})
gOutline = FileAttachment("../java/data/java_outline.geojson").json()
gProv = FileAttachment("../java/data/provinces.geojson").json()
gDist = FileAttachment("../java/data/districts.geojson").json()
gSummary = FileAttachment("../java/data/summary.json").json()
gMapW = Math.min(width, 960)
```

```{ojs}
viewof g3Var = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Plant-available water of the profile, mm", "paw_mm"], ["Clay in the top layer, %", "slcl_top"], ["Organic carbon in the top layer, %", "sloc_top"]]), {value: "paw_mm", label: "Map"})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: gMapW, height: Math.round(gMapW * 0.42),
  projection: {type: "mercator", domain: gOutline},
  color: {type: "linear", scheme: g3Var === "paw_mm" ? "YlGnBu" : g3Var === "slcl_top" ? "Oranges" : "Greens", legend: true, label: g3Var},
  marks: [
    Plot.geo(gProv, {fill: "#f1f1f1", clip: true}),
    Plot.geo(cellFeatures(gCells.filter(d => d[g3Var] != null)).features, Plot.centroid({fill: d => d.properties[g3Var], tip: true,
      title: d => `${d.properties.lat.toFixed(1)}, ${d.properties.lon.toFixed(1)}: texture ${d.properties.texture}, PAW ${fmt.int(d.properties.paw_mm)} mm, clay ${fmt.d1(d.properties.slcl_top)}%`})),
    ...adminMarks(Plot, gProv, gDist)
  ]
}), `module3-grid-${g3Var}`)
```

```{ojs}
g3 = gCells.filter(d => d.paw_mm != null)
```

The profiles hold between ${fmt.int(d3.min(g3, d => d.paw_mm))} and ${fmt.int(d3.max(g3, d => d.paw_mm))} mm of plant-available water, a median of ${fmt.int(d3.median(g3, d => d.paw_mm))} mm, against ${fmt.int(wlSoils.find(d => d.id === "IBMZ910014").paw_mm)} mm for the Millhopper fine sand of the maize experiments. Estimated, not measured: what section 2 showed about the pedotransfer function holds for every cell.

## Self-test

1. GLUE improved the dates of Williams-82 more than its weights. Name two things you would change before
   calibrating again.
2. Why is a GLUE posterior with a wide spread not a failure?
3. Two soils store the same plant-available water, one 60 cm deep and one 150 cm deep. Which would you
   expect to yield more under rainfed conditions, and what in the model decides it?
4. In the rainfed run, where did most of the rain go?
5. What does `ITHRL` = 90% cost compared with 50%, and what does it buy?
